bill.title: Supporting Apprenticeship Colleges Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
bill.officialSummary: Supporting Apprenticeship Colleges Act of 2025 This bill directs the Department of Education to award grants to institutions of higher education that sponsor construction and manufacturing-oriented registered apprenticeship programs for (1) expanding or supporting outreach to high schools, local businesses, local workforce development boards, and apprenticeship intermediaries; and (2) providing advising and support services to students who are enrolled in these apprenticeship programs.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would direct the Department of Education to award grants to colleges and universities that run registered apprenticeship programs in construction and manufacturing. The grants would help these institutions expand outreach to high schools and local businesses, and provide advising and support services to students enrolled in the apprenticeship programs.

industries.rationale: The bill provides federal grants directly to institutions of higher education that sponsor apprenticeship programs.
The bill specifically targets construction-oriented registered apprenticeship programs and would fund outreach to construction businesses.
The bill specifically targets manufacturing-oriented registered apprenticeship programs and would fund outreach to manufacturing businesses.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would order the Education Department to award grants to colleges that sponsor construction and manufacturing-oriented registered apprenticeship programs for (1) expanding or supporting outreach to high schools, local businesses, local workforce development boards, and apprenticeship intermediaries; and (2) providing advising and support services to students who are enrolled in these apprenticeship programs.
plain.whoItTouches: Students, teachers, and the families paying for it.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in school and college. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
